Argyll
ar-GYLE
n. (the western Scottish county of the Campbells, two of whose earls were executed for the Protestant cause in 1661 and 1685)
Gaelic Earra-Ghàidheal, the coastland of the Gaels, from earrann, a portion or coast, and Gàidheal, a Gael.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Argyll is the long western county of sea lochs and islands which was the landing place of the Irish Gaels and the seat of the kingdom of Dalriada; Iona lies off its coast. From the later Middle Ages it was the country of the Campbells, and its earls were among the most powerful men in Scotland. Two of them died on the scaffold for the Protestant interest. Archibald Campbell, eighth Earl and Marquess of Argyll, had led the Covenanting party through the civil wars, crowned Charles II at Scone and then made terms with Cromwell; at the Restoration he was tried on charges arising from that compliance and beheaded at Edinburgh in May 1661, dying with great composure. His son Archibald, ninth Earl, refused the Test Act of 1681 except as it was consistent with the Protestant faith, was condemned for it, escaped to Holland, returned in 1685 in a rising coordinated with Monmouth's, was taken and beheaded in June. The Synod of Argyll meanwhile carried the Gaelic Psalter and the Scriptures to the western parishes. The dictionary records the two executions and declines to make martyrs of them without qualification.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a test as a trial or examination; a scaffold as a stage for execution; composure as calmness; to compound as to settle by agreement; and allegiance as the obligation of a subject.

expand to see more

TEST, n. Means of trial; a standard; that by which the character or quality of anything is tried; an examination.

SCAFFOLD, n. A temporary gallery or stage raised either for shows or for the execution of a criminal.

COMPOSURE, n. The act of composing; a settled state of mind; calmness; sedateness; tranquillity.

COMPOUND, v.t. To settle by agreement or composition; to discharge a claim by paying a part.

ALLEGIANCE, n. The tie or obligation of a subject to his prince or government; loyalty.

Key Scripture

Psa 146:3 — "Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help."

Pro 16:33 — "The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD."

Mic 7:8 — "Rejoice not against me, O mine enemy: when I fall, I shall arise; when I sit in darkness, the LORD shall be a light unto me."

Rev 12:11 — "And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death."

Modern Corruption

Western Scottish county of the Campbells, where Iona lies off the coast, two of whose earls were beheaded in 1661 and 1685 and whose synod carried the Gaelic Psalter to the western parishes.

expand to see more

The corruption to name is the entanglement of a religious cause with a great family's interest, and Argyll is where it is hardest to disentangle. The eighth Earl served the Covenant and also served the Campbell power; he crowned a king he did not trust and then came to terms with the man who had beaten that king, and he was executed for the second rather than the first. The dictionary therefore honours his confession and does not pretend his politics were clean. The warning Scripture gives is against resting a church's cause on any such man: “Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help” (Psa 146:3). A nobleman's protection is a providence to be used and not a foundation to be built on.

The second paragraph gives the ninth Earl his due and states the limit. His offence was a qualification: asked to swear the Test, he swore it so far as it was consistent with the Protestant religion and with itself, and that reservation cost him his head. The dictionary holds that the reservation was right and the rising of 1685 was wrong, for the same reason it holds against Sanquhar and Bothwell. What he had at the end is what the martyrs have: “they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death” (Rev 12:11). The outcomes themselves are God's disposing and not a verdict on the parties, since “The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD” (Pro 16:33), and the right word under such a reverse is Micah's: “Rejoice not against me, O mine enemy: when I fall, I shall arise” (Mic 7:8). The Synod of Argyll's work on the Gaelic Psalter outlasted both earls and both scaffolds.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew nadib-sense of princes in Psalm 146; Hebrew goral (H1486), a lot; Greek nikao (G3528), to overcome.

expand to see more

Hebrew batach (H982) — to trust, to be confident; “Put not your trust in princes”, Psalm 146:3.

Hebrew teshu'ah-sense of help in Psalm 146 — “in whom there is no help”, Psalm 146:3.

Hebrew goral (H1486) — a lot, that which is allotted; “The lot is cast into the lap”, Proverbs 16:33.

Hebrew qum (H6965) — to arise, to stand up; “when I fall, I shall arise”, Micah 7:8.

Greek nikao (G3528) — to conquer, to overcome; “they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb”, Revelation 12:11.

Usage

"“Put not your trust in princes” (Psa 146:3) — a nobleman's protection, not a foundation."

"“the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD” (Pro 16:33) — two earls beheaded, 1661 and 1685."

"“they loved not their lives unto the death” (Rev 12:11) — the Test sworn with a reservation."
